original_value: The enormous financial success of online advertising platforms is partially due to the precise targeting features they offer. Although researchers and journalists have found many ways that advertisers can target---or exclude---particular groups of users seeing their ads, comparatively little attention has been paid to the implications of the platform's ad delivery process, comprised of the platform's choices about which users see which ads. It has been hypothesized that this process can "skew" ad delivery in ways that the advertisers do not intend, making some users less likely than others to see particular ads based on their demographic characteristics. In this paper, we demonstrate that such skewed delivery occurs on Facebook, due to market and financial optimization effects as well as the platform's own predictions about the "relevance" of ads to different groups of users. We find that both the advertiser's budget and the content of the ad each significantly contribute to the skew of Facebook's ad delivery. Critically, we observe significant skew in delivery along gender and racial lines for "real" ads for employment and housing opportunities despite neutral targeting parameters. Our results demonstrate previously unknown mechanisms that can lead to potentially discriminatory ad delivery, even when advertisers set their targeting parameters to be highly inclusive. This underscores the need for policymakers and platforms to carefully consider the role of the ad delivery optimization run by ad platforms themselves---and not just the targeting choices of advertisers---in preventing discrimination in digital advertising.

result.paraphrase: The large financial success of online advertising platforms is partly driven by the precise targeting tools they provide. While researchers and journalists have identified many ways advertisers can target—or exclude—specific groups of users who see their ads, far less attention has been given to the consequences of the platform’s ad delivery process, meaning the platform’s decisions about which users are shown which ads. It has been suggested that this process can “skew” ad delivery in ways advertisers do not intend, causing some users to be less likely than others to see certain ads based on demographic traits. In this paper, we show that this kind of skewed delivery happens on Facebook, owing to market and financial optimization effects as well as the platform’s own predictions about how “relevant” ads are to different groups of users. We find that both the advertiser’s budget and the ad’s content each make a significant contribution to skew in Facebook’s ad delivery. Importantly, we observe substantial skew along gender and racial lines in delivery of real ads for employment and housing opportunities, even with neutral targeting settings. Our findings reveal previously unknown mechanisms that can produce potentially discriminatory ad delivery, even when advertisers choose highly inclusive targeting parameters. This highlights the need for policymakers and platforms to carefully account for the ad delivery optimization performed by ad platforms themselves—and not only advertisers’ targeting decisions—when working to prevent discrimination in digital advertising.
